title: A port call and a visit are different things.
subtitle: One puts you in the harbour. The other puts you in the place.

text: You can call at eleven ports and visit none of them.
sub: A call is a berth and a window of hours. A visit is time enough for the town to stop performing for the ship and go back to its own afternoon.

title: Three ways a call is not a visit

items.head: The two-hour transfer
items.body: The port is a working dock and the city is inland. You see the motorway twice and the place once, briefly.

items.head: The tender-dependent anchorage
items.body: Nothing is promised. Moderate swell, wind or poor visibility suspends the boats and the day quietly evaporates.

items.head: The 07:00 arrival
items.body: You walk a town that hasn't woken, then leave before it has had lunch. Photographs, not a visit.

points.label: First 45 minutes
points.value: Berthing, the gangway, and the walk out through the terminal gate.

points.label: Next two hours
points.value: The transfer in, if the port is not the place you came to see.

points.label: Middle two hours
points.value: The visit itself. One site, one lunch, and no second thing.

points.label: Last 75 minutes
points.value: The transfer back, plus the margin all-aboard quietly demands.

quote: Count visits, not calls. The number is always smaller, and it's the only one that describes the holiday.

title: Send this to whoever you'd share a cabin with.
body: Then send me the itinerary you're weighing up. I'll mark which calls are genuine visits and which are simply berths with a name attached.
